content.text: The text juxtaposes historical anti-Catholic accounts of Inquisition torture, persecution, imprisonment, confiscation, convent abuse, and escapes across Italy, Spain, Bohemia, France, Switzerland, and Naples to England and America, alongside Victorian social satire. In Mugsborough, exploited painters endure poverty, wage cuts, surveillance, unsafe work, unemployment, and hypocritical religious fundraising. Owen explains capitalism’s “Great Money Trick,” showing workers produce goods they cannot afford while owners accumulate wealth. Slyme deceives coworkers, courts Ruth, and later kisses her while she is intoxicated. Easton drinks heavily at the Cricketers Arms, abandons Ruth, and she struggles home before Slyme finds her. The town’s corrupt council manipulates electric-light contracts for private profit. Religious figures preach self-denial while exploiting workers and congregations. Throughout, the narrative criticizes coercive religion, capitalism, class hierarchy, charity, drink, and institutional hypocrisy.
